summary: Psalm 5 opens with a morning plea for Yahweh to hear the speaker’s words and cry. The speaker contrasts God’s rejection of wickedness, lies, bloodshed, and deceit with his own approach to God’s house through loving kindness. The psalm then asks for guidance, judgment against rebels, joy for those who take refuge in God, and blessing for the righteous.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Psalms as prayer under pressure: the speaker brings fear, moral outrage, worship, and hope into speech before God. It also introduces themes common in Book I: enemies, trust, righteousness, and refuge.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” but Davidic headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, collection, or belonging; readers differ on how much biographical certainty they provide.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later adopted by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms are a collection formed over time; assigning one date to Psalm 5 from this chapter alone would be more precise than the evidence allows.
context.setting: The psalm is oriented toward morning prayer and worship toward God’s house and holy temple, while the exact life situation is not named.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, with a musical heading and tightly paired lines of petition, contrast, accusation, and confidence.

outline.heading: Morning Petition
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh to hear his words and cry, addresses God as king, and places requests before him in the morning.

outline.heading: God and Wickedness
outline.note: The psalm states that God has no pleasure in wickedness and rejects arrogance, lies, bloodthirstiness, and deceit.

outline.heading: Approach and Guidance
outline.note: The speaker contrasts himself with the wicked, coming into God’s house by loving kindness and asking to be led in righteousness.

outline.heading: The Enemies’ Speech
outline.note: The enemies are described through mouth, heart, throat, tongue, counsels, transgressions, and rebellion; the speaker asks God to hold them guilty.

outline.heading: Refuge and Blessing
outline.note: The psalm closes by asking joy for those who take refuge in God and by affirming blessing and favor for the righteous.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh, in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I will lay my requests before you, and will watch expectantly.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the chapter as morning prayer and gives the speaker’s posture: request joined to expectation.

keyVerses.text: But as for me, in the abundance of your loving kindness I will come into your house. I will bow toward your holy temple in reverence of you.
keyVerses.why: This verse marks the turn from God’s rejection of wickedness to the speaker’s approach to worship.

keyVerses.text: Lead me, Yahweh, in your righteousness because of my enemies. Make your way straight before my face.
keyVerses.why: This is the central request for guidance in the presence of enemies.

keyVerses.text: For you will bless the righteous. Yahweh, you will surround him with favor as with a shield.
keyVerses.why: The final verse summarizes the psalm’s confidence that God protects the righteous with favor.

questions.question: What is the opening line before the prayer doing?
questions.answer: Verse 1 includes a heading: “For the Chief Musician, with the flutes. A Psalm by David.” headings can name performers, genres, instruments, collections, occasions, or associations, and their exact historical force is debated. Here it signals a musical or worship setting, but it does not by itself prove a recoverable performance scene.

questions.question: Why does the speaker pray “in the morning”?
questions.answer: The chapter itself presents morning as the time when the speaker expects Yahweh to hear his voice. Verse 3 does not command every reader to pray only then; it depicts this speaker laying requests before God and watching expectantly at the start of the day.

questions.question: What does “meditation” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse, “meditation” appears alongside “my words” and “the voice of my cry,” so it belongs to the speaker’s prayer language. The text does not define it further. A cautious reader can say only that the speaker asks Yahweh to consider what is voiced or pondered before him.

questions.question: Does the psalm say God hates people?
questions.answer: Verse 5 says, “You hate all workers of iniquity,” while verses 4-6 also say God has no pleasure in wickedness, that evil cannot live with him, and that Yahweh abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man. Readers differ over how to explain this language: some stress God’s opposition to evildoers, while others emphasize the poetic and judicial force of the psalm’s speech. The severe wording expresses divine judgment and does not authorize personal hatred.

questions.question: What is “your house” and “your holy temple”?
questions.answer: Verse 7 says the speaker will come into God’s house and bow toward God’s holy temple. Many psalms are oriented toward Jerusalem and its temple, while some speak from unnamed personal crises. This verse gives temple-oriented worship language, but the text does not tell us the exact date or physical circumstances behind the prayer.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask to be led because of enemies?
questions.answer: Verse 8 asks Yahweh to lead the speaker in righteousness and make his way straight “because of my enemies.” The next verse describes the enemies’ speech as faithless, destructive, tomb-like, and flattering. The request is not simply for information; it is for a straight path when hostile or deceptive voices surround the speaker.

questions.question: Is verse 10 a prayer for revenge?
questions.answer: Verse 10 asks God to hold the enemies guilty, let them fall by their own counsels, and thrust them out because they have rebelled against God. This is an imprecatory request: the speaker hands judgment to God in strong language. Responsible readers differ on how such prayers should be used later, but the chapter itself presents the plea as an appeal to divine judgment, not as the speaker taking vengeance directly.

questions.question: Who are “all those who take refuge in you”?
questions.answer: Verse 11 widens the focus from the speaker to all who take refuge in God, love God’s name, and are defended by God. The psalm does not identify them as one institution or group by name. Within the chapter, they are contrasted with rebels and workers of iniquity, and they are invited into joy.

questions.question: What picture does “favor as with a shield” give?
questions.answer: Verse 12 says Yahweh will bless the righteous and surround him with favor as with a shield. The image presents favor as protective surrounding, not merely approval as an idea. It closes the psalm by moving from request and danger to confidence in God’s protection.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that points to a musical or worship-related setting; the exact ancient role is not explained in the chapter.
Instruments named in the heading; the chapter preserves the direction but not the ancient melody or performance details.
The quality by which the speaker says he will come into God’s house, emphasizing God’s generous mercy in this verse.
The place toward which the speaker says he will bow in reverence; the chapter uses temple-oriented worship language without giving a date or occasion.
The action of those who are invited to rejoice in verse 11; in this psalm it means looking to God for defense.
